title: Morning and evening protection
hook: in the name of Allah, with whose name nothing harms, three times (Abu Dawud; Tirmidhi)
tomorrow: what does it mean to be 'pleased' with God, out loud?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the master of forgiveness: Your favor and my sin, side by side, with no 'but'. You are my lord. Today, a line for the two edges of the day.
screen: `YOU ARE MY LORD.` → `THE EDGES OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Lock the door, check the stove, check the lock again: the small ritual at the edge of the day that says, let nothing happen tonight. The Prophet ﷺ gave one, said three times in the morning and three in the evening: bismillahil-ladhi la yadurru ma'a ismihi shay'. In the name of Allah, with whose name nothing on earth or in the sky can harm, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. So, one question for today: can words keep you safe?
screen: `CHECK THE LOCK AGAIN.` → `THREE TIMES, MORNING AND EVENING.` → `CAN WORDS KEEP YOU SAFE?`

segments.voice: The hadith, in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, comes from Uthman ibn Affan: whoever says it three times in the evening won't be struck by a sudden affliction until morning, and three times in the morning, until evening. Then comes the most human detail in the report, and it's worth telling someone tonight. The man passing it on, Uthman's son Aban, was later struck by a partial paralysis, and someone stared at him. Aban said: the hadith is as I told you, but on that day I was angry, and I forgot to say it. He didn't hide the hard case. He told it inside the hadith. So the tradition's answer isn't a charm. The line begins with a name, bismillah, and puts the day under that name. Now a neighbor who keeps the same two edges. In Jewish tradition, the Shema is said evening and morning, following the Torah's words about speaking God's words, in the JPS translation, "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Two traditions, the same two edges of the day, the same instinct to begin and end with God. And one honest difference: the Shema's words come from the Torah itself and declare that God is one; this Muslim line comes from the Prophet's sayings and asks for protection, counted out three times. Neither has to be the other. Nothing harms with his name.
screen: `THREE TIMES, AT EACH EDGE.` · `THE NARRATOR WHO FORGOT.` · `THE SHEMA: LYING DOWN, RISING UP.` · `ONE HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `NOTHING HARMS WITH HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: Say the line three times, aloud and slowly, in Arabic or in English: in the name of Allah, with whose name nothing on earth or in the sky can harm, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. If you don't pray, sit instead with the question underneath it: what am I handing over tonight that I can't guard myself? Let the quiet hold the answer.
screen: `THREE TIMES, ALOUD.` · `WHAT CAN'T I GUARD MYSELF?`

howItsDone: Muslims who keep the morning and evening remembrances (adhkar) say this line three times after the dawn prayer and again in the evening.
